cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable for longitudinal attrition (no panel or cohort follow-up), though 23% item non-response on race/color in 1996-2014 SIM/DataSUS mortality records creates substantial missing-data uncertainty in the mortality numerator (PDF pp. 13-14).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Serious / High concern: Empirical analyses rely exclusively on unadjusted national bivariate percentages and raw counts from separate, unlinked Census and DataSUS tables without age-standardized mortality rates or adjustment/stratification for region, municipality, urban-rural residence, or household income/socioeconomic status (PDF pp. 11-15).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate (narrative-doctrinal framing only): Accurately cites Brazil's 1988 Federal Constitution (arts. 196, 200, 225), Basic Sanitation Law (Law 11.445/2007), Statute of Racial Equality (Law 12.288/2010), and PNSIPN (2013) to establish de jure sanitation and health rights, but institutional/environmental racism and state non-enforcement are conceptualized theoretically and historically rather than operationalized as a measurable legal or regulatory exposure variable (PDF pp. 3, 6-8, 11).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern: Self-declared IBGE/SUS race/color categories (combining Black and Mixed into the Black population) and Funasa/Costa et al. DRSAI disease lists are explicitly defined, but 23% missing race identification in DataSUS mortality records, acknowledged SUS disease underreporting, and omitted exact IBGE adequacy thresholds and ICD-10 extraction codes introduce measurement and classification uncertainty (PDF pp. 4, 9, 11-15).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate / Adequate descriptive administrative indicators: Basic sanitation deficits (water supply, waste collection, sewage disposal/treatment, no household bathroom) and DRSAI deaths/hospitalizations draw on official national 2010 IBGE Census and SIM/SIH DataSUS registries, but outcomes are presented as raw counts and within-deficit racial shares rather than population-standardized incidence/mortality rates, with unstated technical coding cutoffs (PDF pp. 11-15, 22).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern: No pre-registration or analysis protocol exists for this exploratory study; selected descriptive indicators (2010 Census sanitation shares, 1996-2014 DRSAI mortality shares, and a single summary count of 2008-2016 hospitalizations without racial comparisons or denominators) are reported without sensitivity analyses for the 23% missing-race death records (PDF pp. 5, 11-15, 23).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern: Historical and sociological literature was selected via non-systematic exploratory bibliographic research without search terms or inclusion rules (PDF p. 5), and while quantitative tabulations cover full national Census/DataSUS universes, excluding the 23% of 1996-2014 DRSAI deaths lacking race/color data from racial proportion calculations introduces potential differential missingness bias (PDF pp. 13-14).

domain_ratings.justification: Accurately cites primary Brazilian constitutional and statutory provisions governing health, environment, basic sanitation, and racial equity—specifically the 1988 Federal Constitution (arts. 196, 200, 225), Law No. 11.445/2007 (Basic Sanitation Law), Law No. 12.288/2010 (Statute of Racial Equality), the 2013 National Policy for Holistic Health of the Black Population (PNSIPN), and the 2001 Durban Declaration—though legal analysis remains high-level and does not dissect specific regulatory or municipal enforcement provisions.

domain_ratings.justification: Clearly specifies the national Brazilian legal and public-health jurisdiction (SUS, Funasa, IBGE) and frames its claims at the macro-national scale, while explicitly acknowledging in the Final Considerations that regional, local, and subnormal-cluster variations are not disaggregated here and require future localized research.
domain_ratings.where_found: Introduction (PDF pp. 3, 5); Black population's environmental health in sanitation (PDF pp. 11-15); Final considerations (PDF p. 18)

domain_ratings.justification: Explicitly defines the Black population following IBGE and SUS demographic convention as the sum of self-declared Black and Mixed (pardo) categories (Footnote 2) and defines institutional and environmental racism conceptually via Geledés (2013a), Werneck (2016), and Bullard (2004, 2005); however, state institutional omission or legal non-enforcement is not directly operationalized as an empirical variable distinct from aggregate racial group membership.

(2004), WHO ICD manuals, and Funasa (2015) in Footnotes 9 and 10.

domain_ratings.justification: Literature and historiography were gathered via non-systematic 'exploratory-level bibliographic research according to Gil (2009)' without search strings, databases, or inclusion/exclusion criteria, and in the 1996-2014 DataSUS mortality dataset 23% of the 231,087 DRSAI deaths lacked race/color information and were dropped when computing racial mortality proportions (55% Black vs. 43% white), creating substantial completeness and selection uncertainty despite the author's candid discussion of this missingness.
domain_ratings.where_found: Introduction (PDF p. 5); Black population's environmental health in sanitation (PDF pp. 13-14)

domain_ratings.justification: Reports exact counts and racial percentages for 2010 Census sanitation inadequacy (Figure 1) and 1996-2014 DRSAI mortality (Figure 2), lists included DRSAI diseases (Footnote 10), and credits an IBGE/RJ technician for statistical extraction of the Census data; however, exact IBGE variable recodes separating adequate from inadequate sanitation, exact ICD-10 code queries in Tabnet DataSUS, and the arithmetic behind the 'every hour and a half' fatality metric and 'almost 2 million' hospitalizations are not fully detailed.

domain_ratings.justification: Presents historical narrative synthesis alongside unadjusted cross-sectional national tabulations from separate, unlinked datasets (2010 IBGE Census for sanitation access; 1996-2014 and 2008-2016 DataSUS for DRSAI mortality and hospitalizations); there is no empirical linkage between legal/policy exposure, sanitation deficits, and health outcomes, nor any quasi-experimental or multivariable design to identify causal effects.

overall_narrative_summary: Study S239 (de Jesus, 2026; English translation of a 2020 Saúde e Sociedade article) is a political-historical and legal-institutional sociological study examining environmental and institutional racism in Brazilian sanitation and environmental health. Methodologically, it combines non-systematic 'exploratory-level bibliographic research' on colonial slavery historiography, Brazilian constitutional/statutory sanitation and racial-equality guarantees (1988 Constitution arts. 196, 200, 225; Law 11.445/2007; Law 12.288/2010; PNSIPN 2013), and institutional racism theory with purely descriptive macro-tabulations of national secondary data from the 2010 IBGE Census (racial shares of populations lacking water supply, waste collection, sewage treatment, and bathrooms) and Tabnet DataSUS (1996-2014 SIM mortality and 2008-2016 SIH hospitalizations for Diseases Related to Inadequate Environmental Sanitation, DRSAI). Under the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework (structured non-validated judgment), its strengths lie in rich historical-institutional contextualization (D10 strong), explicit researcher reflexivity (D13 strong), and clear conceptual/nosological definitions of sanitation deficits and DRSAI categories (D4 strong), alongside accurate high-level citation of Brazilian statutes (D1 adequate) and national administrative universes (D2, D5, D7, D11 adequate). However, for empirical or causal inference, it has major methodological limitations: bibliographic selection is non-systematic and 23% of 1996-2014 DRSAI death certificates lacked racial identification (D6 weak); Census and DataSUS tabulations are unlinked and unadjusted for age structure, region, urban-rural status, or income/socioeconomic confounding, relying on group shares rather than age-standardized population rates (D8, D9 weak); and exact Census recoding rules and ICD-10 query scripts are not reported (D12 weak).
overall_rating: Structured non-validated judgment: Weak for causal/inferential attribution; Adequate for descriptive national disparity documentation and legal-historical institutional contextualization (no numeric composite score)
study_design_identified: Political-historical and legal-institutional sociological case study combining exploratory bibliographic/historical synthesis with descriptive secondary macro-tabulations of national census and public-health administrative data (2010 IBGE Census and 1996-2016 DataSUS)
where_found_summary: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Introduction — legal framework, study aims, researcher reflexivity, and exploratory methodological statement (PDF pp. 3-5); Theoretical & legal-policy sections on institutional and environmental racism (PDF pp. 6-9); Historical & quantitative empirical section using 2010 IBGE Census and 1996-2016 DataSUS with Footnotes 9-10 and Figures 1-2 (PDF pp. 9-15); Final considerations — limitations and call for future quantitative/qualitative research (PDF pp. 16-18); References, Acknowledgement, Funding, and Data availability (PDF pp. 19-23).
why_tool_chosen: The article integrates a legal-policy and colonial-to-present institutional-historical analysis of Brazil's sanitation and health framework (1988 Constitution, Law 11.445/2007, Law 12.288/2010, PNSIPN 2013) with unlinked, purely descriptive macro-tabulations of national 2010 IBGE Census and DataSUS administrative records. Because it uses non-systematic 'exploratory-level bibliographic research' (ruling out AMSTAR 2), collects no primary qualitative interview/field data (ruling out CASP/MMAT), evaluates no specific policy intervention comparator (ruling out ROBINS-I), and performs no individual-level analytical cross-sectional regression linking exposure and outcome (ruling out JBI Analytical Cross Sectional), the 13-domain Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework is the most appropriate instrument.
